newsitem.title: USA: Viacom preserves appeal right in Seagram ruling.
newsitem.headline: Viacom preserves appeal right in Seagram ruling.

text.p: Viacom Inc has preserved its right to appeal last month's Chancery Court decision favoring Seagram Co Ltd in the dispute over their joint partnership in USA Networks.

According to papers made available to Reuters Wednesday, Vice Chancellor Myron Steele agreed not to enter a final judgement on his May 15 decision, thus preserving Viacom's right of appeal. He also agreed to Viacom's stipulation that there be no appeals until 30 days after he issues a court-ordered plan for the dissolution of the partnership.

Steele ruled last month that Viacom had violated a non- compete provision in the USA agreement. He gave both sides 30 days to come up with a consensual plan for dissolving the partnership or 45 days for separate plans.

The first deadline has passed, and separate plans are now due June 30. A Viacom spokeswoman declined comment on whether the companies are still in talks. Both sides will have until July 11 to respond to each other's proposals, after which Steele will fashion a plan for dividing the USA partnership assets between the partners.
In his 55 page decision, Steele indicated how he may lean in devising his Solomonic remedy.

He disagreed with Viacom's contention that a buy-sell provision in the partnership agreement would unfairly favor Seagram. "Nothing in the record convinces me this is true. The buy-sell mechanism...allows an independent investment bank to set a fair market value for the venture. There is no reason to conclude the existence of a wide disparity in the buy-sell offers, assuming the initiating offer to have been reasonably calculated," Steele said.

He also rejected Seagram's position that it would face a severe tax burden if forced to sell its share to Viacom. "While the tax consequences may be severe, given the resources the parties are able to bring to bear on the issue, I see no reason why a sale under either of these scenarios could not be constructed to at least minimize tax liability," Steele said.
